en: Oṃ, homage to Bhāratī!
Victorious is the goddess Sarasvatī, by whose grace poets of subtle intellect behold the surface of the world as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of their hand.

"Are you exhausted? Let go of the mountain; we shall carry it," said the cowherds as they slackened their arms, which had been outstretched and bent by the weight; while they spoke thus, the laughing Hari is victorious.
May that Dāmodara protect you— he whose folds of skin shine forth, creating the illusion of lines from being bound by an exceedingly firm rope.
Victorious is he upon whose head shines the crescent moon, placed by me with longing like a silver shell,
as if desiring to seize the collyrium reflected in his eyes.
The good person who has extensively proclaimed the virtues of others attains even greater good fortune;
the radiance of the moon, causing the night-lotuses to bloom, carries a twofold luster.
"The wicked person is even more treacherous than a venomous serpent"—this which the wise say is no falsehood;
for while that [serpent] hates only the mongoose, the slanderer hates the entire family. (SuVas 6)
In an exceedingly foul task, the intellect of the wicked becomes remarkably skillful;
for the sight of owls attains its form only in the darkness.
Just as a hand soiled with dust, the more it rubs against a virtuous person,
the more it makes him— like a mirror— possess a stainless luster.
The wickedness of the base becomes exceedingly foul when they destroy the virtues of others;
even the clouds, though they obscure the light of the moon, possess a greater darkness within.
Its flavor has been destroyed, the young lotuses wither, and the crane does not move about;
for Vikramāditya has passed from the earth into legend alone, like a lake that remains only as a memory.
Even when its virtues are unknown, the speech of a true poet pours forth a stream of honey into the ears;
for even before its fragrance is perceived, a garland of *mālatī* flowers captivates the gaze.
Even for those possessing qualities, the realization of their own true nature occurs only through another;
for the vision of one's own majesty arises in the eyes only upon the surface of a mirror.

Subandhu, who received the grace of a boon granted by Sarasvatī, and who is the sole kinsman of the virtuous, composed this literary work— a composition consisting of wordplay at every syllable— as a treasury of skill in artistic arrangement.
1) There was one who had never existed before,
whose jewel-like toenails were polished by the friction of the tips of the whetstones that were the crest-jewels of the entire circle of sovereigns of the earth;
who, like a lion among men, displayed the wonder of his gift of the field of Kaśipu.
Like Kṛṣṇa, he had performed the satiation of Vasudeva;
like Nārāyaṇa, he had easily acquired the circle of the earth; and like the enemy of Kaṃsa, he had produced an abundance of joy for Yaśodā.
Like Ānakadundubhi, he took delight in poetry;
like one reclining upon the ocean, his feet were adorned by the crest-jewels of the infinite serpent-king;
and like Varuṇa, he was the protector of the quarters.
Like Agastya, he was the subduer of the southern quarter;
like the ocean, he was the leader of hundreds of rivers (armies) and possessed the movement of sea-monsters (elephants);
and like Hara, he was followed by Mahāsena and had conquered Māra.
Like Mount Meru, he was the abode of the wise and the refuge of Viśvakarman;
like the sun, he delighted in bestowing light and dispelled the heat of shadows;
and like the flower-bannered god of love, he produced unobstructed prosperity and bestowed the bliss of delight.
The Vidyadhara was well-disposed,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra was fond of virtue, and Sudharmāśrita was followed by patience.
Though possessing the majesty of Bṛhannalā, he was inwardly straightforward;
though born of a queen, he was a progenitor of bulls (or a producer of virtue); and though not fickle, he was a great leader—the king named Cintāmaṇi.
2) And wherever he governs the circle of the earth, there are the employment of deception and suppression in debates,
atheism among the Cārvākas,
and the application of thorns [punishment] in administrative duties.
Slander among lute players, association with the wicked among rice fields,
and the harboring of double-tongued serpents among snake-charmers.
The cutting off of hands for those who pay fixed taxes, the plucking out of eyes for sages, and hostility toward kings for lotuses— these are the fates of those who act improperly.
The yoga of all the stages belongs to the elephants of the quarters; the conjunction of the trident occurs at the birth of a young woman;
and the purification by fire and scales pertains to gold.
In the *Mahābhārata*, there is the sight of Duḥśāsana;
for aquatic creatures, there is the splitting by saws;
such is the supreme established order.
The Great Boar, though intent on uplifting the earth, caused its destruction; Rāghava, though avoiding the land of Janaka, entered the forest together with the daughter of Janaka;
and Bharata, though manifesting devotion toward Rāma, brought an end to his own sovereignty.
Even though Nala had already been united with Damayantī, he again took possession of the earth;
likewise, Pṛthu expanded the circle of the earth by displacing the mountains.
Thus, there is no occasion for speech regarding these even more ancient kings.
3) Furthermore, he was indeed different from all previous rulers of the earth;
for instance,
by displaying the rising of his horns, he took delight in the *gandharvas* who move everywhere within his camp, never ceasing to do so.
That Himālaya is not merely a mountain from which frost rises, nor is it beneficial for the birth of Māyā;
for he is the proud mountain upon whom the bull-bannered Lord resides, and he is the true goal.
Having cleared away the entire wilderness,
he is the foremost of purifiers;
he is not eager for worldly enjoyments, yet he is most captivating to the mind.
That ocean Ratnākara is not composed of water; how then can it be unfathomable and possessed of boundaries?
There was no excessive wonder even at this;
for it was the abode of the moon, composed of nectar,
and a worthy recipient.
His anger is immovable; he is like a great river,
and he is that ocean together with its boat.
Like the moon, he brings delight to the night;
he is the kinsman of the lily groves and the abode of the entire multitude of arts.
The ocean, whose power is not overcome by enemies, is the cause for the rising of friends; bearing a golden splendor, it shines.
His sovereign glory was as unshakable as Mount Sumeru;
moreover, his host of enemies— though they were the Pārthas— were never fit for a great Bhārata-like war,
and even Bhīṣma was not devoted to the welfare of Śantanu’s lineage.
Even with his followers, he was not adorned by the lineage;
moreover, like Triśaṅku, he stood outside the path of the stars,
yet even as Śaṅkara, he was not despondent.
Though he was fire, his path was not black;
though he consumed his substratum, he did not burn;
and unlike Death, he did not suddenly snatch away life.
He was not like Rāhu, whose splendor increases by seizing the orb of the sun; nor like Nala, who was ruined by the play of Kali;
nor like Viṣṇu, who rejoiced in the praise of killing a jackal.
Like Nanda the cowherd, he was accompanied by Yaśodā; like Jarāsandha, he was skilled in both peace and war; like Bhārgava, he was ever devoted to giving and enjoyment.
Like Daśaratha, he was accompanied by Sumitrā and presided over by Sumantra;
like Dilīpa, he was followed by Sudakṣiṇā and protected by Guha;
and like Rāma, he brought forth Kuśa and Lava and possessed a towering form.
And he was like the Pārijāta tree, bringing joy to those who sought refuge;
like the Himālaya, producing auspiciousness; and like Mount Mandara, marked by the coils of the serpent.
Like Mount Kailāsa, it had been enjoyed by Maheśvara;
like the city of Madhura, it brought joy through various gardens; and like Mount Mandara rising for the churning of the Ocean of Milk, it made the world resound with its fame.
With his delight aroused like the rope of passion,
he was like a mass of Īśāna’s power rising at twilight;
with a heart as pure as an autumn cloud, he was one who clung to the foot of Viṣṇu.
Like Pārtha, he was accustomed to the daring of battle; like Kaṃsa, he was adorned by the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa;
and like Tārkṣya, he brought joy to Vinatā and delighted Sumukha.
Like Viṣṇu, he had embraced a beautiful woman; like the son of Śantanu (Bhīṣma), he had brought the law of time under his own control;
like the Kaurava battle-array, he was presided over by Suśarman.
Subāhu, though a delighter in Rāma, was impartial toward all;
though a devotee of Maheśvara, he possessed equal vision for everyone; and though free from worldly attachment, his inner nature remained steady.
Like a cloud that terrifies the royal swans with its streams of exceedingly pure water,
there was a son named Kandarpaketu, a lamp of his lineage whose ten virtues remained unimpaired.
4) And by him, who— like the moon— is the abode of the entire multitude of arts, who captivates the night, and who is the kinsman of the lily groves;
With their desires gratified,
they gazed upon the oceans as if they were mountains with shimmering peaks,
having cast their lives far behind them.
The worlds of living beings, being serene in nature, attained supreme prosperity—
those who were born from him whose play was unceasing and who was fond of delight.
At the sight of him, who was like the god whose bow is flowers— the one with the dolphin-banner— the hearts of women leaped with joy;
and for him, who was followed by the ever-flowing southern wind, [the people gathered].
To him whose voice was as soft as the song of the cuckoo, which brings delight to the eyes and ears;
who had caused the sprouts to blossom; and who had created waves of lovely ripples.
To him who is delightful with fragrant flowers, who possesses lotuses easily accessible to all people,
and who has the excellence of outstretched hands;
Just as for springtime, which has surpassed the damanaka season,
forest creepers are crowded with thousands of buds and frequented by bees.
The young women, whose youth was radiant, longed for those who carried coral;
and on the field of battle, his staff-like arm [held] the bow.
From the bow came arrows;
by the arrows, the heads of enemies;
and by those as well, the circle of the earth.
By him the Leader was never before experienced;
by the Leader, fame;
and by fame, the seven oceans.
Through the oceans, there was the recollection of the conduct of kings beginning with the Kṛta Yuga;
by this [ocean], stability was attained, and by that [conduct], a wonder was encountered at every moment.
And the region of whose enemies' breasts was abandoned by their pearl necklaces— as if out of fear of being struck by the palms of their hands, which had been scorched by the fire of his majesty;
and whose surroundings were bristling with pearls fallen from the frontal globes of intoxicated elephants shattered by his iron arrows,
while the birds were darting about— [The text continues...]
It was crowded with hundreds of blooming white lotuses in the form of crocodiles and elephants moving through the waters of blood;
it was filled with dancing headless trunks,
and was terrifying due to the mass of haughty posturing by warriors eager for union with celestial beauties.
In the lake of battle,
the sword shone, drenched in the blood of foot-soldiers, elephants, and horses, as if stained by the red lac-dye from the feet of the Goddess of Victory.
5) Then, once the night had subsided, when the mass of foam from the Yamunā of night— white as curd and like a lump of food for the mendicants of time— had gathered,
Within the circle of shade cast by the honeycomb, like a fragment of stone used for rubbing away the nails of Menakā,
his head rested comfortably upon the pillow of the western mountain;
he was like an earring resting upon the remaining honey.
As the lord of the night-lotuses— desirous of the luster of a conch shell— sinks into the waters of the western ocean like a drinking cup for the bride that is the night,
his rays become like feet caught in the midst of the frost-dusted pollen of the night-lotuses.
In the six-legged bees,
in the sārikā birds startled by the awakening of their lovers' amorous chatter,
and in the monasteries where the teachers were active in their duties, [the night passed].
The streets resounded with the poetic tales sung by mendicants whose mouths were parched with hunger;
they seemed to vomit forth the mass of nocturnal darkness that had been entirely consumed, unable to endure its extreme thinness under the guise of soot,
and appeared weary from repeatedly stretching their necks as if to catch a glimpse of the amorous dalliances of couples.
In those [lamps] which were witnesses to the various amorous sports within the dwellings that served as the abodes of diverse wise men;
which, like one who has sought refuge, swallowed the darkness lurking below;
and which, like the words of the wicked, had reached a state of dullness due to the burning away of their oil.
Like those who have reached the end of their lives when excessively aged,
like those whose lords have perished and remain as mere vessels,
like Dānavas wandering the paths of the night;
The lamps were like the setting suns fallen upon the peaks of the western mountain,
resonant with the humming of swarms of bees made vocal by the intoxication of a continuous flood of flower-nectar drops.

While the floral offerings in the bedchamber were withering away, and while the women— whose locks of hair, like jasmine blossoms fallen from their heads, seemed to shed teardrops out of grief for separation from their lovers as if to forbid the departure of their beloveds— were making their lotus-feet talkative with anklets;

and while the spray of summer water was being drunk by the breeze from the wings of swarms of humming bees, greedy for the fragrance of *mālatī* garlands crushed in their tresses that had loosened from the exhaustion of lovemaking at night’s end;
In those [courtesans] made beautiful by the jingling sound of their tossing vine-like arms;
whose garments were whitened by the radiance of milk-white teeth emerging as whistling sighs produced by the pain of fresh nail-marks, bitten lips, and the shedding of hair;
and who were being gazed upon at every moment by their circle of friends, distressed by their inquiries for a chance to see their beloved once more.
In those women, whose modesty was momentarily stirred by the sweet talk of the house-parrots which recalled hundreds of bold words from their lovemaking at night;
who, with breasts adorned by nail-marks, resembled the splendors of autumn days;
and who, facing the city of the Lord of Life, were as if on the verge of death.
Like rows of spring forests abounding in buds,
as amorous women were embraced by their lovers,
the filaments of flowers were shaken.
In that lake of blooming white lotuses, which was a mine of joy and frequented by charming female bees humming amidst the pollen of filaments,

the god of love— acting as a distributor of misery— rained down, as it were, a shower of embers upon those women separated from their lovers, who were themselves devoid of happiness, while he himself was filled with pride.
While the wind, beloved by the *kokila* birds, blew far-reaching, [the lady] was adorned with her hips—
which served as the archway for the city of Love and the golden rampart for the temple of the great treasure-house of the God of Desire.
With the circular basin of her creeper-like hair, with the halo surrounding the orb of the moon in the sky,
and with the golden plate of the line of hair that serves as an inscription of victory over the three worlds;

Her hips were encircled by a girdle-string that served as a moat for the captive dwelling of the hearts of all people, and which was like a rod for the play of the eyes of the world; she appeared as if exhausted by the sorrow of not being able to behold her face hidden by the weight of her high breasts, or as if fatigued by the pressure caused by the jars of her heavy hips and breasts.

She was adorned with a waist that had become exceedingly slender, as if from the thought, "How shall the fall [of my gaze] be directed toward me alone? or as if from the resentment of having taken a heavy wife, or as if from the exhaustion produced by the touch of the Creator’s hand as he oppressed her excessively.
Her breasts were adorned with nipples like gems of passion set in gold, which,
due to their extreme heaviness and fullness, seemed as if pinned down by the Creator under the guise of the nipples out of fear of their falling,
and which possessed the residual beauty of all her other limbs poured into them.
[Like two lotuses from the lake of the heart, like the playful movements of the two Cupids dwelling within the chest, like the two fruits upon the vine of the line of body hair,
and like two oceans filled with the subduing powder that increases the pride of Kandarpa.]
By those two which have produced veneration by falling into the hearts of all people without exception;
which are the fruits of the great tree of saṃsāra; and which are the blossoms of the great tree of youth.

She was resplendent with her two breasts, which were like two *cakra* birds alluring with their pearl necklaces as if they were lotus stalks; which appeared like the fruits of the trees at Prayāga under the pretext of contact with the pearl necklace and the line of body hair; and which served as secluded dwelling-houses for the god of love when he was exhausted by the toil of conquering the three worlds.
With the continuous glow of twilight clinging to his moon-like face,
which resembled the vermilion seal of protection for his jewel-like teeth,
it was as if colored by the passion of his heart streaming forth.
She was graced by a sprout-like lower lip that resembled a fragment of coral from the ocean of passion;

with her long, thick-lashed, tremulous, and languid eyes— resembling the petals of a young *ketaka* flower— she created the illusion of a window for the playful lover dwelling in the temple of her heart, an eye that,
though full of passion, produced liberation.
As if enraged by the obstruction of its course, it reddened its edges and seemed to whiten the entire world;
it made the sky appear as if filled with a forest of blossoming lotuses.
She was adorned with a pair of eyes that seemed to vomit forth thousands of oceans of milk and that mocked the splendor of the beauty of jasmine, blue lotuses, and *mālatī* garlands;

she was further embellished by a bridge-like nose, which served as a jeweled balance-beam for her teeth and acted as a tethering post for the elephant of youth and passion, having been raised upon the dam of her eyes.

She was resplendent with her two creeper-like eyebrows, which were like rows of bees upon the blue-lotus eyes, like the two arches over the gateway of the temple of the God of Love, like two streams from the ocean of passion,
and like two female dancers in the performance of youth.
She possessed lovely breasts that shone like the beauty of the sky during the rainy season;
she stood with her feet placed upon anklets that tinkled like the joyful shouts of a populace celebrating a victory;
and her eyes rested upon her ears like the steadfast resolve of Suyodhana.
Displaying folds of skin like the playful dwarf-incarnation of Viṣṇu, having transcended the signs of Virgo and Libra like the position of the scorpion in the zodiac,
she was like Uṣā, who found the joy of beholding Aniruddha.
Like Śacī, she possessed the luster of eyes worthy of adoration;
like the dance-play of Paśupati, she had shimmering serpents for her eyes;
and like a forest, she had lofty, dark breasts.
She was like the army of the monkey-king, graced by the body of Sugrīva;
she possessed feet as gentle as Saturn, a heavy yet pleasing appearance,
hips that were deep red like the lower lip, eyes that were fully blossomed, and was adorned with radiant ornaments.

She was like a painting upon the wall of worldly existence composed of the planets; like a meeting ground for the beauty of the three worlds; like the perfected elixir of the collyrium of aesthetic flavor (rasa) for youth;
like the creative faculty of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra);
and like a treasure-trove of curiosity.
Like a victory banner for the god of the sea-monster emblem,
like the triumph of the two beloveds of Love,
and like a meeting ground for loveliness.
Like a powder for paralyzing the senses,
like the power of enchantment belonging to the God of Love,
and like a pleasure garden of beauty;
Like a single-chambered hall of good fortune,
like the place of origin of loveliness,
and like the perfected mantra for attracting the mind.

In a dream, he beheld a maiden about eighteen years of age, who was like a great medicinal herb for binding the eyes of the magician Kama, and like a polishing stone for the eyes of Prajapati upon the three worlds; then, drinking her in as it were with eyes wide with joy, he gazed upon her.
6) Then, as if drinking her in with eyes expanded by affection, he gazed upon her.
As if out of jealousy toward his birth, sleep—long practiced—deserted him;
yet once awakened, he was unable to steady himself, feeling as though he were submerged in a lake of poison or in the words of a wicked man.
For instance, with both arms outstretched for a moment to embrace the expanse of the sky, he cried: "Come, come, my dearest!"
"Do not go! Do not go! he cried, as if his beloved were inscribed in every direction and intermediate quarter, carved out, or fixed within his eyes and buried in his heart.

Then, hiding right there on the surface of the bed, having forbidden all his attendants from seeing him, having bolted the door, and having abandoned all enjoyments such as betel and food, he passed that day.
In the same manner, he spent the night as well, longing for a union with her in his dreams.
7) Then his dear friend, named Makaranda, having somehow managed to gain entrance, spoke to Kandarpaketu, who was helpless under the blow of Kāma’s arrow:
"Friend, why have you resorted to this improper conduct, fit only for the wicked?
Seeing this behavior of yours, virtuous men dwell upon it, swaying on the swing of doubt."
Furthermore, the wicked perceive each such undesirable thing as being precisely improper;
the heart of a wicked person consists of the very essence of exposing what is undesirable.
Who indeed is capable of determining his true nature?
For instance: Bhīma is not a hater of Baka;
the fire, though it consumes its support, is the wind;
and that which is exceedingly bitter is yet a great flavor.
Like mustard oil, even when rubbed between the palms of the hands or borne upon the head, it does not abandon its pungency.
Like the juice of the palmyra fruit, it is sweet at first taste but bitter and unpleasant in its final transformation.
Like the pollen of a tree, it causes a sense of distress to the heads of men, even though it has been shaken off.
Like the fruit of a poison tree, the more it is experienced, the more it only strengthens delusion;
it does not produce a thirst for water, like a low-lying region. Like a summer day, envy carries away the distress of even those with refined minds.
Like darkness, he was adept at following after faults; like Viśvakarman, he was intent on destroying all craftsmanship; though possessing eyes, he was deformed (Virūpākṣa);
and like Indra, though bearing a discus, he praised those born in the lowlands like the horse Ucchaiḥśravas.
Even when pierced like an arrow, it displays affection;
it churns the heart like buttermilk;
and like an offering to a yakṣa, it is noisy with its own clamor and speaks of wandering in circles.
Like an intoxicated elephant, his mouth is restless with its own will and he has cast aside the gift of generosity;
like a bull, he is impaired by the wandering of his senses and is devoted to the path of the perverse;
and like the disorder of indigestion, he brings about a dullness even in speech within his body.
Like a deceiver, he is attached [to others] yet yields bitter fruit; like one infatuated with the night, he is devoted to darkness; like a departed spirit, he perceives the misfortune of his kin;
and like an axe, he hews down even the most auspicious prosperity.
Like a spade that cleaves the earth, he tears asunder those who possess forbearance;
like a pleasure-post, even when engaged in the lowest acts, he puts the virtuous to shame;
and like a wicked straw-eater, though delighting in the forest, he does not approve of even the abundant grass that follows him.
From no seed at all, sprouts of ruin for the field arise and spread from no stalk; they become difficult to eradicate.
For even a tiny fragment of a fault, once entered into the heart of the wicked, becomes terrifying;
it does not enter the heart of the virtuous at all.
If he should somehow enter again, he would not remain for even a moment, like quicksilver;
for virtuous men, like deer weary from the hunt, seek only the drop of diversion.
Indeed, people such as you bring happiness, like the autumn season, and being conscious, they do not offer advice that is inconsistent with their friendship.

Even for insentient things, there is a form of friendliness when they are placed within a compatible category; for instance, water—even though it is insentient—diminishes as if having reflected: "Since milk, by virtue of its sweetness, coolness, purity, and capacity to soothe heat, has attained the status of being 'milk' through the cause of its association with me, and since it has increased upon meeting with me, it is only right that its destruction should occur first in my presence during the boiling process. Thus, even water diminishes as if by this very thought.
"This conduct of yours is most improper. Friend, take the path appropriate for virtuous people;

for even the virtuous may, through delusion, set out upon a wrong path," and so on. While he was speaking thus, Kandarpaketu, rendered helpless by the blows of the God of Love, somehow spoke in measured words:
“Friend, the mental state of a virtuous person becomes as agitated as Diti was by Śatamanyu.
This is no time for instruction;
my limbs seem to be burning and my senses seem to be boiling.”
The vital points seem to be pierced;
the life-breaths seem to be escaping; discernment seems to be uprooted.

"My memory has vanished as if lost. Therefore, if you are now one who played with me in the dust and shared in my joys and sorrows, then follow me," he said; and, unnoticed by his attendants, he departed from the city together with him.

Immediately thereafter, having traveled a distance of several hundred *nalvas*, [he reached] that mountain which possessed thousands of peaks brought forth from the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) by the word of Agastya.

Its slopes were crowded by hundreds of Śabaras eager to kill the herds of yak-cows who were delighted by listening to the songs of pairs of Vidyādharas sleeping happily in the vine-bowers within the mountain caves;
its rocky surfaces were perfumed by breezes carrying the fragrance of yellow sandalwood that was being pulled down and crushed by the trunks of the elephants on the ridges;
and it was filled with throngs of monkeys eager to taste the sap from palm fruits broken by falling from a great height.

Its surroundings were made fragrant by the scents of the juices of various fruits being sipped by pairs of *jīvañjīvaka* birds perched upon excellent sandalwood trees from which waterfalls were cascading down;

with its peaks variegated by pearls fallen from the frontal globes of intoxicated elephants torn open by the sharp edges of the claws of thousands of impetuous lions, it bore the appearance of a head adorned with a cluster of stars;
and like Sugrīva, its shade at the base was frequented by bears, gavayas, *śarabhas*, lions, and *kumudas*.
Like Paśupati, he had ashes raised by the breath of serpents;
like Janārdana, he wore a variegated forest garland;
and like the thousand-rayed sun, he was accompanied by chariots drawn by horses with seven-striped tails.
Like Virūpākṣa, he had Guha stationed nearby and was followed by Śiva;
like a lover, he was accompanied by the passion of the forest and possessed of Madaṇa;
and like Śrīparvata, Mallikārjuna was stationed near him.
Like Naravāhanadatta, he was attended by a queen dark as the priyaṅgu plant;
like an infant, he was supported by his nurse;
and like the beginning of day, the rows of forest trees on his slopes were flushed with the rosy glow of the dawn.
He was like the dark fortnight, dense with thickets of creepers;
like Karṇa, who had experienced the gift of a hundred koṭis;
and like Bhīṣma, marked by crescent-headed arrows released by Śikhaṇḍin.
Like the arrangement of the *Kāmasūtra*, he was delighted by the beautiful forests fashioned by Mallanāga;
like Hiraṇyakaśipu, he took refuge in the lineage of Śambara;
and under the guise of the red hue of ochre, he was attended by Aruṇa as if for the purpose of seeking the path of the sun’s chariot above.
With his eyes wide open by the sun and moon situated upon its peaks, he seemed to be gazing toward the path of Agastya;
with the coils of aged pythons like entrails hanging down,
he resembled Kumbhakarna with a host of monkeys caught between his teeth.
There stood a ketaki bower, which served as a rendezvous for the courtesans of Indra’s consorts, whose paths were indicated by rows of footprints marked with red lac; it was like one who,
though of low birth, is adorned with a noble lineage,
and who, though displaying fearlessness, brings about the fruit of death.
Though possessing a *prastha* measure, he is immeasurable;
though accompanied by a drum, he is soundless; and though fearsome, he is a friend to the *kīcaka* reeds.
The great mountain named Vindhya was seen, though covered by garments, yet shimmering with silken cloths; for it,
by virtue of its thickets of shrubs, displayed various transformations of mineral ores,
and like a virtuous man, its greatness was made manifest through the gracious conduct of its followers.
Like the logic of Mīmāṃsā, it obscured the teachings of the Digambara [Jains];
and like the *Harivaṃśa*, it was made beautiful by the manifestation of Puṣkara;
and like masses of stars, it was joined with Pisces, Gemini, and Cancer.
Its borders were adorned with ponds containing cranes, elephants, bhadra-birds, and young bakula trees, as if by musical instruments;
and it was [further] graced by [trees] variegated with blossoms,
from which leaves fell like bamboo slips.
He displays manifold playful variations of meter through *sukumāralalitā*, *puṣpitāgrā*, *śikhariṇī*, and *praharṣiṇī* verses, like a grove of creepers.

Furthermore, he dwells by a river whose waters are made fragrant by the mass of honey-drops falling from clusters of blooming lotuses shaken by the broad tails of *bhākūṭa* birds, which are startled by the warbling of intoxicated *kalahaṃsa* and *sārasa* cranes; and whose waters have been drunk from the navel-regions of royal beauties emerging at the time of evening twilight.

Its banks and sandbanks were made resonant by the clamor of flocks of royal swans crying out with passion; its waters were thickened by streams of ichor flowing from the temples of herds of intoxicated elephants near the shore;

and its groves along the bank bore witness to the amorous dalliances of youthful divine couples resting comfortably upon the sandbanks formed by the heaps of pollen fallen from the groves of *ketakī* trees growing on the banks.

Its waters were being plunged into by water-deities dwelling within pavilions formed by clusters of rose-apple trees fallen near the hollows at its banks; it was a place where the enjoyment of celestial couples—drawn there out of curiosity by the "kuhu-kuhu" cries of flocks of gallinules hiding amidst the reed-canes growing on the shore—was being refined; and its banks resounded with the clamor of flocks of wild cocks and jungle-fowl born along the river's edge.
Its soft sandy banks were trampled by water-dwelling humans; its waves were made tremulous by breezes from the groves;
and its half-hidden śaphari fish were being watched by the wives of baka-cranes perched within the thickets of reeds.
It possessed a terrifying cane forest where fish were seized by hawks greedy for their offspring;
its waters near the banks were adorned by rows of extremely swift leeches fleeing upon seeing the staff-bearers moving amidst the waves;
and its shores were being excavated by hundreds of Kirātas, who, out of curiosity to seize hidden treasures, had been captivated by the mating of pairs of *khañjarīṭa* birds.
With a facial contortion as if in anger, with a faltering gait as if intoxicated,
and with an increasing momentum like the Fortune of Daybreak at its onset.

He was embraced by the Revā river, which was like the battlefield of Bhārata with its dancing headless trunks (*kabandha*), like the rainy season with its expanding lotuses concealing venomous serpents, and like the pursuit of wealth and pleasure through service to kings; she was his beloved, embracing him with her outstretched hands of waves. And he—
Even now, with the roars of elephants mangled by the tips of Hari’s sharp claws upon their frontal globes,
his arms— reaching as high as *tāla* trees— seem to summon the Pot-born Sage [Agastya].
Then Makaranda said to him:
"Behold, a lion of cruel form, with his body bent upward and downward in its hind and fore-quarters respectively, with his stiffly arched back and his tail-tip slightly curved and raised;
with the cavity of his mouth made formidable by the tips of his fangs, shaking his thick mane, and with ears pricked, he paces toward the lord of elephants."
Moreover,
this lion— ears pricked, his mane bristling with fierce intensity, his body formidable with a cruel and terrifying form, bearing his stiffly erect tail,
and crouching with all his limbs drawn in upon the frontal globes of the head of a mountain-cave elephant that is trumpeting— is such that he cannot be depicted even in a painting. 16.
10) And immediately thereafter, [the army] proceeded like a river in a low-lying region with its banks thickened by *nyagrodha* trees;
like a battlefield for the northern conquest of cattle with its sprawling great *nalas*;
and like a caravan of camphor merchants on a journey through the Maru desert with its flow of *ghanasāra*.
It was like a refined assembly of honey-drinkers, with the wine of various creepers;
it was like the mental state of Nala’s chariot-pole, constantly supporting Rambhā; and it was like the gait of an intoxicated elephant, its path made known by the ringing of bells.

Having walked a few steps through the Vindhya forest— which, like service rendered to a lord, yielded abundant fruit after rising far above; and which, like the fortune of Virāṭa, delighted hundreds of Kīcakas—
he, marked by the shafts of Love like a lover, [beheld...]
Like the son of Vikartana (Sūrya) with his glossy radiance,
like Vaikuṇṭha bearing Lakṣmī, and like a king setting out on a military expedition adorned with a thick canopy;
He rested in the shade at the foot of a rose-apple tree, which was adorned with many branches like the Veda, and radiant with numerous shoots like the art of singing.
11) In the meantime, the Blessed One, the garlanded with rays, ascended the peak of the western mountain, his orb as ruddy as the eyes of a buffalo exhausted and intoxicated by the heat.
12) Then Makaranda, having gathered fruits and roots, somehow managed to provide him—who was averse to the practice of eating—with food;
and he himself partook of what remained after he had eaten.

Then, gazing upon that very beloved one inscribed upon the tablet of his heart with the brush of his imagination, Kandarpaketu— his faculties overflowing with emotion— slept upon a bed of sprouts fashioned by Makaranda.
Then, when the night had been divided by only half a watch, he heard the clamor of a parrot and a maina quarreling together on the top of a rose-apple tree.
Kandarpaketu said to Makaranda,
"Friend, let us first listen to their conversation.
Then the sarika spoke in words tremulous with indignation.
“You have returned after searching for another female śārika bird, gambler; otherwise, how could so much time have passed for you during the night?
Hearing this, Śuka said to her:
“Noble lady, I have heard a story never heard before.
Then, being pursued by her as curiosity arose within her, he began to tell it:
“There is [a city] adorned with statues, white with excellent plaster like the supporting pillars of the *Bṛhatkathā*.”
They were like meters accompanied by the play of young students,
like herds of elephants with rutting bulls,
and like the armies of Sugrīva with Gavākṣa.
It was illuminated by houses with well-constructed lower floors that resembled the palaces of Kubera;
it was graced by a Dhanada, a Pracetas, and a Rāma who was a protector of his subjects.
By Priyamvadā, who was like the flower-bowed god of love; by Bharata, the slayer of enemies;
and by him who, though devoted to the lunar days, was inclined toward honoring guests.
Though he was beyond counting, he was counted among the virtuous;
though he was a most heroic piercer of vital points,
he had not fallen into attachment to various intoxicants.
By the Sudarśana [discus] even though it is wheel-less;
by the Supratīka [elephant] even though he is free from pride; and by the Haṃsa [swan] even though he is without wings.
By him who, though a lamp of his lineage, had not yet extinguished his affection; who, though a connoisseur of the essence of poetry, was free from grasping;
and who, like a summer day, possessed an ever-increasing brilliance.
Like the month of Māgha at the time of its conclusion, he was one who had commenced his ascetic penance;
like the wind, he was one who traveled upon the right path;
like the sun, he was a protector of the earth.
It was followed by the local inhabitants who bore the moon like Maheśvara;
it was like a mass of rain clouds with its circle of coral jewels;
and it was as if accompanied by a host of celestial women, refined by their intimacy with Indrāṇī.
Like a wild elephant with the luster of fresh sprouts,
like a cuckoo nourished by others,
and like a bee cherished among flowers;
Like a leech skilled at drawing out blood;
like a frequent sacrificer seeking sexual pleasure;
like the arm of a great dancer grasping a serpent.
There stood the city named Kusumapura, presided over by courtesans who were like Garuḍas causing distress to the hearts of the playful, or like the demon Andhāsura risen above the tridents;
there, whose lotus-feet were caressed by the garlands of jewels from the crowns of gods and demons.

The Blessed Goddess Kātyāyanī, known by the name Caṇḍā, herself dwells there; she whose lotus-feet are washed by the streams of the Gaṅgā falling from the matted locks of the bearer of the Ganges as he bows in devotion, and who is a flame of forest fire to the great forest of the army of Śumbha and Niśumbha, and a vajra-razor-edge to the great mountain-like Mahiṣa Asura.
In whose vicinity flows the river that carries the fragrance of the pollen from the garlands of flowers on the crowns of gods and asuras,
which is a stream of the liquid of dharma from the water-pot of Prajāpati,
and which serves as a meritorious rope for the hundred sons of Sagara to ascend to the city of the gods upon the surface of the earth.

Its shores were shaken by the flanks of Airāvaṇa; its waters were made fragrant by the flow of yellow sandalwood; its waves were set trembling by the impact of the rounded hips of playful celestial nymphs;
and its sacred stream was perfumed by the forest of matted locks of the Seven Sages, which had become pure from the garlands they wore while descending to bathe.
Her hair was curled in locks due to the latent impressions produced by wandering within the hollows of the matted locks of Shiva, who bears the crescent moon as his forehead-mark;
she was capable of enduring the touch of the hands of a universal monarch, like the earth itself;
and like a lake in the rainy season, she was inferred to possess water-lilies and white lotuses submerged in its depths by the swarms of bees circling above, blinded by their scent.
She was like the science of prosody graced by the *mālinī* meter,
and like a row of planets adorned by the son of the Sun (Saturn) while possessing royal swans;
she was like the splendor of an autumn day, with its radiant red lotuses (*kokanada*) and its blossomed white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*).

The divine Bhāgīrathī flows on—though she has destroyed the blinding darkness, she is yet possessed of [cosmic] darkness; though her waters are ruffled by waves, she is difficult to traverse like the Avīci hell.
And [she flows] with those who, in every direction, bear clusters of stars like heaps of flowers.
With clouds uplifted;
with sprouts made uneven by the grazing of the sun’s chariot-horses, who were overcome by the lash-strokes of Anūru;

and possessing the delusion of untimely twilights, as they were adorned with thousands of delicate, fresh shoots grown thick from being sprinkled by clusters of nectar-drops transferred to their feet, which were as beautiful as the moon’s army.
It was as if inhabited by the deeds of Bharata accompanied by Sītā; it was as if filled with great heroes bearing coconuts;
it was as if populated by unrefined youths with eyes cast far ahead.
They were like ascetics intent on silent recitation;
they were as if adorned with garlands;
and they were like lions with manes bristling upward, ready to rend the frontal globes of elephants.
It was graced by the trees of the grove, which, though possessed of the signs of death, were long-lived; and though joined by sages, were nonetheless presided over by the god of love.
It was inhabited by many families of gods like the womb of Aditi;
it was graced by the great Bali and presided over by serpents like the netherworld (pātāla); and it was more sacred even than the abodes of the gods.
It was undisturbed even by serpents.
There, his long arms were marked with the impressions of jeweled earrings from women who had fallen asleep, exhausted by the weight of amorous play;
and his lotus-like hands were made fragrant by the scent of the flower-garlands from the tresses of the Fortune of fierce adversaries.

There dwells a king named Śṛṅgāraśekhara, who, like a fertile field, accomplishes many purposes; who, like Pārtha, is accompanied by Subhadrā and Bhīmasena; and who, like Kṛṣṇa, is joined with Satyabhāmā.

He who is Indra, the slayer of Bala; Agni, the purifier; Yama, the King of Dharma; Nirṛti; Varuṇa, the wise one; Vāyu, the ever-moving; Kubera, the giver of wealth; and Śaṅkara—though possessing these eight forms, he is yet of undiminished form.
He is the protector of the gods, yet his heart is solely devoted to supreme merit; he is a planet, yet he delights in the path appropriate for a Guru (Jupiter).
His hand bears an exceeding friendship with the hundred-peaked [mountain], and as a giver of all possessions, he treats even the Lord of the Gods like a blade of grass; thus he is victorious.
On the field of battle, he performed the summoning of the life-force of his enemies with his bow; the foe became breathless, and his arrows attained their mark. By that, he acquired fame;
"forgiveness" was released by him and swiftly accepted by the enemy hosts with their heads. That lord of the earth did not reach another state than death while stationed amidst the hostile army.
And while that king, clever in statecraft, was ruling the earth— this world girt by the four oceans— he performed the *vṛṣotsarga* (the release of a bull) for the ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*),
the moon entered the signs of Virgo and Libra,
and there was deliberation regarding the *śūlaghāta* and other such astrological conjunctions (*yoga*).
The movement of the right and left hands is for determining directions;
the piercing of arrows is for curdling milk;
and the binding with chains is for the composition of letters.
The figure of speech *utprekṣā* has been discarded among poetic ornaments; there is a falling away from the granting of rewards for arrows;
and there is the total destruction of *kvip* suffixes.

The closing of the sheath occurs in the beds of lotuses, not in flower garlands; the loss of noble birth occurs in base families, not in flowers; the loss of passion occurs in aged elephants, not in men.
The presence of discoloration occurs in bamboo flutes and the like, not in the loveliness of beautiful women;
the interruption of the Gāndhāra note occurs in musical scales, not among the women of Pāṭaliputra; and the attainment of fainting occurs in songs.
The absence of dust is found among lowly servants and not on their garments; the wearing of soiled clothes occurs at night and not among people;
and fickleness of passion exists in songs and not among wise men.

There was a loss of virility in the amorous sports, but not among the citizens; there was fragility in the transformations of passion, but not in their hearts; there was bodilessness in the god of love, but not among his attendants.
The arrival of Māra occurs at the onset of youth, not among natural dispositions; the slaughter of twice-born ones occurs during sexual unions, not among subjects;
the binding of a girdle occurs in amorous quarrels, not in acts of giving.
Redness was found in the lips of young women, not in their attendants;
cutting was found in the hair and eyebrows of women, not in their husbands; and cruelty was found in swords.
The destruction of the sword stood supreme among warriors;

and his queen was like a streak of ichor from a world-elephant, delighting the rows of bees [or her subjects], and like Pārvatī, she was both delicate and adorned with a crescent moon [or a digit of the moon].
She was like a row of forest trees, radiant with jasmine blossoms and variegated;
she was like a host of celestial nymphs, with beautiful, well-groomed hair and a most charming voice;
she was the foremost of the entire harem, named Anaṅgavatī.
And while those two were in their middle age, by some stroke of fate,
a daughter named Vāsavadattā was born to them— her form capable of enchanting the three worlds, who delighted the thousand-eyed Indra like the daughter of Puloman.
Then she remained averse to marriage, even as her youth reached its full maturity, like a creeper that has been raised upon the forest of Rāvaṇa’s arms.
Now, on one occasion, the heat of passion was aroused in travelers by the humming of swarms of bees falling upon the clusters of blossoming mango buds;
and the quarters of the sky were filled with the warbling of sweet-voiced cuckoos, whose throats were rendered hoarse from tasting the nectar of mango flowers stirred up by the gentle Malaya breeze.
The lotus ponds were made resonant by the clamor of flocks of intoxicated kalahamsas sporting amidst the clusters of blooming lotuses;

the hearts of the wives of travelers were grievously wounded by the southern breeze, which was laden with a spray of droplets from streams of honey flowing from the openings of pāṭala buds torn by the tips of cuckoos' claws;
and the bakula trees were made to bristle with joy by the sprinkling of wine from the mouthfuls of amorous women delighted by the intoxication of spring.
Where hundreds of *kaṅkeli* trees were delighted by the intense blows from the lotus-feet—tremulous and formidable with the anklets—that blossomed under the sway of the god of love;

where hundreds of travelers were bewildered by listening to the *carcarī* songs commenced by a multitude of *khiṅga* men who were eager for their ears to hear songs consisting mostly of obscenities in every direction;
and which, like a wicked man, was devoid of the lotuses of the virtuous.
Like one of low birth from a base family,
like Rāvaṇa attended by hundreds of yellow and red-leafed palāśa trees,
and like a great lover carrying a fragrant scent.
Like a virtuous king, he possessed a flourishing realm;
like reality itself, his hopes for happiness increased;
and like the composition of a great poet, he was bound by no defects.
Like a virtuous man, he was free from the persistence of faults;
like a fisherman, he wore a garland of bound blue and white lotuses; and like a flock of birds in a flourishing lake, he despised the maruvaka flower.
Like Śakra, beloved by Indrāṇī;
like the Great Hero, having subdued Damana; and like a libertine, ever-charming and unflagging—the spring season arrived.
20) Who in this world is not transformed by honey that has grown exceedingly strong, since even the Sage, though he was liberated from passion (*atimukta*), blossomed?
A swarm of bees clinging to the base of the fresh mango shafts of the Flower-Arrowed One shone as if with a leaf.
A bee humming within the opening of a jasmine flower emerging from its stalk made a sound like the blast of the conch for the world-conquest of the Fish-Bannered God (Kāma).

Under the influence of its passion for the blows from the feet of young women—feet adorned with anklets and made crimson by fresh lac-paste—the *aśoka* tree bore that very same redness in the guise of its new sprouts.
The *bakula* tree shone, bearing within its own flowers the essence of the nectar, as if out of passion for contact with the lotus-faces of amorous women whose mouths hummed sweetly with honey.

Here and there, the cluster of *kaṅkeli* blossoms, dappled by swarms of bees alighting upon it, resembled the circle of a funeral pyre for the half-extinguished God of Love, and it brought burning anguish to the hearts of travelers.
The row of blooming blue lotuses shone like a necklace of sapphire and pearls variegated by swarms of bees belonging to the Goddess of Spring.
The *nāgakeśara* flower was as beautiful as a discus of the Flower-Arrowed God for the purpose of crushing the hearts of women separated from their lovers.
The *pāṭali* flower appeared like a banner of the Fish-Flagged One to seize the hearts of travelers on the road.

21) It possesses the quality of sweetness enriched by the fragrance arising from the contact with the dense braids on the broad foreheads of Lāṭī women, who are intent on the perfection of amorous play;
it carries the scent of the saffron dust from the jar-like breasts of beautiful women, lovely in their mastery of the arts of love;
and it makes the vault of heaven resonant with the most sweet humming of swarms of bees that have joined it through the fragrance transferred by the tossing of the locks of hair of longing beloveds.

The Malaya breeze blew, skilled in the art of tracing patterns upon the cheeks of Kerala women tremulous with the passion of fresh youth; it was adept at massaging the rounded hips of Mālava women whose faces were refined by mastery in the entire collection of the sixty-four arts; and it was cooled by droplets of perspiration from the heavy burden of their firm breasts, which pressed closely against their feet due to the exhaustion of amorous play.

In the meantime, Śṛṅgāraśekhara, having learned the intention from the circle of Vāsavadattā’s friends, assembled all the kings who rule over the entire surface of the earth for the sake of his daughter’s svayaṃvara; [an assembly] made resonant by the thick humming of swarms of bees, which were delighted by the fragrance of burnt black aloe-wood,
and intermingled with the radiance of the flashes of their exceedingly impetuous laughter.

Vāsavadattā ascended the dais, which was crowded with people skilled in various conversations and full of amorous sentiment; it was thronged by swarms of bees from the city gardens attracted by the fragrance of burning incense; and it made the horizons resound with the sound of the *nandighoṣa* drum, like the battlefield of Arjuna.
23) Among them, some were like sprouts of the arts that had conquered the ornaments of the city;
others were like the Pāṇḍavas, anointed with divine vision and black aloe-wood;
and others were like autumn days, in which the quarters of the sky had grown vast.
Others were as if prepared to seize him, seeking their own strength;
some were like hunters listening for the cry of a bird,
while others proceeded like trackers following a form.
Some, like those who hear the doctrine of Jaimini, were destroyers of the Tathāgata’s teaching;
some, like wagtails, were merely observers of the results of the year;
and some, like the regions surrounding Mount Sumeru, were composed of gold.
Some, like beds of night-lotuses, closed their eyes at the sight of the Sun;
some, like swans, were convinced that it was a magical illusion produced by the vision of the Cosmic Form;
and some, like the Suvāhas, though powerful, sought to restrain themselves with the thought of self-protection.
Some, though desiring to take her hand, considered it difficult to do;
some remained steadfast even after being surpassed; and some, like the sons of Pāṇḍu, had their patience stolen away by ignorance of the secret of the dice.
Some were like Guṇāḍhya, authors of the Bṛhatkathā;
some were like winds, having gone into the state of animals; and some were like the Kaurava soldiers who betrayed Droṇa.
Some of the princes stood for a moment like beds of white water-lilies unable to endure the light;
and that maiden, having gazed at each one of them for a moment, descended from her litter.

24) Then, in that very night, she saw in a dream one who was adorned by Aṅgada like Vālin; whose neck was captivating like the moon at the beginning of the dark fortnight; and who was as skilled in attracting beautiful women as the golden deer.
Like Jayanta, he delighted the elder gods (Vṛddhaśravas) with the nectar of his speech; like Kṛṣṇa, he did not fail to bring joy to Kaṃsa;
and like a great rain-cloud, he was radiant with his hand (or thunderbolt).
Like the great ocean, he was a Great Being,
with Mālinī as his female attendant and Tuṅgabhadra as his nose.
With his lower lip like the Śoṇa river, with speech like the Narmadā, with arms like the Godāvarī, and with fame like the celestial Gaṅgā, he was as if composed entirely of merit.
The primary root of the tree of erotic sentiment,
the Rohaṇa mountain for the entire collection of jewels of virtue,
and the source-mountain of the rivers of beautiful narratives.
The fragrant month for the mango tree of cleverness, a mirror-surface for the face of goodness, and the primary root of the creepers of knowledge.
The self-chosen husband of Sarasvatī,
the dwelling place of rivalry between Fame and Fortune,
and the primary abode of the perfections of virtuous conduct.

She beheld a youth whose form was as enchanting to the three worlds as a treasury of great beauty. (25) In that very dream, she heard his name and other details: "He is the son of King Cintāmaṇi, named Kandarpaketu. Immediately thereafter, she thought: "Oh, how marvelous is this craftsmanship of the Creator in fashioning such beauty!

"I suspect that this [Nala] was fashioned by the Lotus-born [Brahmā], whose mind was eager to behold the beauty of his own craftsmanship, by gathering the atoms of form from the assembly of the three worlds; otherwise, how could he possess such a distinction of loveliness?
In vain indeed did Damayantī undergo the calamity of dwelling in the forest for the sake of Nala."
In vain did Queen Indumatī remain devoid of passion;
fruitlessly did Śakuntalā experience the curse of Durvāsas for the sake of Duṣyanta;
and in vain did Madanamañjukā desire Naravāhanadatta.

"Without cause, she desired Nalakūbara, who had surpassed Rambhā with his vast majesty; and fruitlessly, Dhūmorṇā longed for Dharmarāja amidst the thousands of gods, grahas, and gandharvas who had come for the svayaṃvara"— thinking thus in many ways, she felt as if she had entered the midst of the embers of separation,
as if seized by the fire of Kālāgnirudra.
As if entered into an underground cavern,
as if painted upon a deserted village,
as if carved out.
As if bound in chains,
as if joined with adamantine cement,
as if entered into a cage of bones.
As if situated within the vital points,
as if variegated with the essence of marrow,
as if permeated by the life-force.
She considered Kandarpaketu to be as if presiding over her inner self, as if liquefied within the seat of her blood, and as if distributed throughout her very flesh.
Like one insane, like one deaf,
like one mute.
As if empty, as if the collection of senses had been cast away, as if seized by a swoon;
As if seized by a planet,
as if overwhelmed by a succession of waves from the ocean of youth, and as if obstructed by the ropes of passion;
As if pinned down by the flower-arrows of Kandarpa,
as if reeling from the poison of erotic passion, and as if transfixed by the barb of contemplating her beauty;
"O dear friend Anaṅgalekhā, as if my life were struck by the Malaya breeze, place your hands and feet upon my heart;
O charming Madanamañjarī, sprinkle me with sandalwood water; O simple Vasantasenā, bind up this mass of hair like a noose!"
O Taralā, scatter the pollen of the *ketaka* flower, Lavangavatī; O Mālinī, enough with the *śaivala* leaves;
O fickle Citralekhā, paint in your picture that person who steals the heart.
"O spirited Vilāsavatī, scatter this heap of pearl-dust; O passionate Rāgalekhā, cover the fullness of your breasts with a cluster of lotus leaves;
O lovely Kāntimatī, gently wipe away these teardrops. [Yūthi...]
Now that Yūthikā has passed away, waft your breezes moist with lotus petals;
come, O Blessed Sleep, and show me your favor.
"Fie on my other senses! Why were my limbs not made entirely of eyes by the Creator?
O Lord Kusumāyudha, here is my salutation with joined palms; you are my follower."

"O Malaya breeze, teacher in the initiation for the longing of love, blow as you wish upon such a person as she!"— speaking thus in many ways, Vāsavadattā fainted along with her circle of female friends.
Immediately thereafter, her life was restored by the efforts of her attendants.
At one moment on the sandy banks of rivers flowing with the pollen of exceedingly cool camphor;
at another moment on the shores of streams filled with the thick, cold dust of Malaya sandalwood;
and at another moment in the shade of trees on the banks of lakes surrounded by groves of lotuses.
For a moment in groves of plantain trees with leaves stirred by the breeze,
for a moment on beds of flowers,
and for a moment on spreads of lotus petals.
For a moment she was led by her attendants upon stone slabs cooled by masses of snow;
yet, being consumed by the fire of separation— fierce as the mass of rays from twelve suns risen at the time of universal dissolution—
she bore a body exceedingly emaciated, like that of the Brahmins.
Her lotus-face had its sprout-like lower lip suffused with a white smile like the mass of waves tossing in the ocean of sorrow, stirred by the swaying Mandara mountain;
her pair of eyes was devoted to the twice-born (or the Vedas) like a flock of birds;
and the beauty of her nose-bridge, extending far out, seemed as if it wished to inhale the fragrance of the natural perfume of her face.

Her row of teeth was as delicate as a digit of the moon freed from its spot, and as white as a mass of nectar-foam; her beauty surpassed even that god of love, the likes of which had never been seen before.
"Blessed are those places and those regions,

and blessed are those syllables of his holy name which partake of the merit of his good deeds, since they have been adorned by him"— thus reflecting again and again, she felt as if the very quarters of the sky were inscribed with these thoughts.
As if carved into the sky,
as if reflected in the eyes,
as if painted upon a canvas.
She remained there, gazing at it as if it were something she had seen before.
Then her female parrot, named Tamālikā, having consulted with her friends, set out to ascertain the state of Kandarpaketu’s feelings;
she returned and, saying, "She is standing right here beneath this very tree along with me," she fell silent.
28) Then, rising with joy, Makaranda informed Tamālikā of the news; she, having offered her salutations, presented the letter to Kandarpaketu. Thereupon, he read it himself.
For even a woman who has seen her lover with her own eyes is fickle-hearted;
a young woman whose experience was in a dream does not establish firm conviction.
29) Having heard that, Kandarpaketu, as if immersed in an ocean of nectar and standing above all joys, rose very slowly and, stretching out his pair of arms, embraced her.
Then, seated together with her, [he wondered], "What is she saying? What is she doing?"
Asking her the entire account, beginning with "How did you remain? and so forth, Kandarpaketu passed that night and the day as well, and then set out.
In the meantime, the blessed Lord Marīcimālī (the Sun) descended to the middle world as if to narrate this very event.

Then, bearing a slowness as if out of the transfer of his own heat to the circle of *cakravāka* birds, the orb of the day—reddened like a copper-crested cock (*tāmracūḍa*)—became beautiful like a cluster of *mandāra* blossoms.
Bearing the graceful illusion of the frontal globes of Indra’s elephant smeared with vermilion;

possessing a navel-circle resembling a jeweled earring upon the coils of the formidable Vāsuki, which served as a beautiful binding for the mass of Śiva’s matted locks tossed upward by the fierce momentum of his *tāṇḍava* dance;
and lovely like a garment of fresh lac-dye at the junction of twilight.
Possessing the luster of the jeweled locks of the courtesans of Varuṇa’s city,
it had the circular form of the headless trunk of Day severed by the Sun;
it was like a skull-cup filled with honey belonging to Kālakapālin.
Like a cluster of unfading blossoms of Fortune,
like a cluster from the Ashoka tree of the sky,
and like a golden mirror for the graceful lady of the western quarter.
Like Balabhadra joined with Vāruṇī, he was both passionate and intoxicated;
like a pauper who has lost all his wealth, he was both dejected and destitute;
and like a Śākya, he wore garments of red silk.
Accompanied by Saṃjñā, the Blessed One sank into the waters of the final ocean, appearing like a massive coral reef tossed up by the force of the restless waves.

Gradually, he reached the mountain peaks, which were made resonant by the clamor of flocks of kalaviṅka birds distressed by quarrels over their nests as they scrambled up from the dust; meanwhile, the crows there were longing for a place to dwell.
In the dwelling chambers where the fragrance of burning black aloe-wood incense issued incessantly;
where the elders, enraged by the clamor of children eager to hear the stories being narrated by clever folk gathered in circles on banks strewn with *dūrvā* grass, were intent on silencing them;
and where the pleasure of light hand-clapping was provided by old women whose tongues were as restless as their dangling anklets as they recounted tales.
While the children were desiring to sleep,

while the low-born women displayed the gestures of the God of Love, and while the learned men sat for their twilight prayers— rendering them unpleasant by hearing the various vulgar words of the slave-girls pursued by lustful men;
In forest glades where the backs of the most gentle herds of deer were occupied by families of animals sluggish from rumination;
in the garden trees where the nests were filled with flocks of *droṇa* birds no longer asleep due to their longing for sleep;
and when the family of owls, the householders of their huts within the hollows of ancient trees, was desiring to depart.
While the flickering lines of lamp-light emerged as if to threaten the darkness, appearing like the rays of the sun entering a fire;
and while the god whose banner is a sea-monster, having drawn his bow taut, incessantly rained down a multitude of arrows that steal away the intellect of the entire world;
and while [the night] was graced by the preparations for the commencement of love-making.
While the servants were occupied with the speech of the procuresses,
while the women were chattering as they fastened the networks of girdles upon their hips,
and while the courtyards were filled with the haste of storytellers departing for their homes due to the suspension of their continuous discourse;
In garden plots where cocks have been settled,
and where peacocks have been made to climb upon poles;
In the courtyards of houses where the time for the twilight prayers had been established,
swarms of bees lay within the hollows of the buds of lotuses— spaces made narrow by the tips of their filaments rising in contraction;
meanwhile, the divine Sun was about to proceed along this path, while Varuṇa, as it were, fashioned a carpet from all the jewel-paved floors.
It was like a stream of blood from a wild buffalo slain by the Blessed One at the proper time; it was like a coral vine from the great ocean of the sky;
it was like a red lotus-pond of the celestial lake.
Like a golden bridge for Kandarpa,
like a crimson banner of madder-dye upon the palace roof of the sky,
and like the Goddess Lakṣmī herself when she has chosen the yellow-robed Viṣṇu in a svayaṃvara;
The blessed twilight appeared like a female mendicant dyed with passion for the stars, or like a lady wearing crimson garments;
and in an instant, the sky— now empty of the scales-holder (Tulādhāra)— resembled a marketplace street where the twilight-disciples, skilled in the art of adorning the night, were like courtesans.
In the lotus ponds, the clusters of petals were becoming densely closed, while the bees wandered here and there in the lotus pools as if they were the very hands of darkness.
While the lotus-ponds seemed to lament, as it were, through the pretext of the broken cries of female ospreys, distressed by separation from the sun;

and at the hour of evening, which, like an astrologer, indicates the stars.
Resembling the throat of Śiva, dark with its thorny stalks; like the army of the Daityas, with its stars clearly visible;

like the Nandana grove, where the owl (kauśika) wanders;

It was as if pregnant with life upon mountain slopes as hard as dense stone;

as if inflamed by the spray from the streams of rut flowing from the temples of elephants, which were darkened by swarms of bees clinging densely to them;
and as if gathered into a mass within the shadows of the widespread groves of *mālatī* and *tāla* trees.
It was as if dissolving into the coils of serpents dark as collyrium-juice,
a cloak for the harlot Night,
and a grey-hair remedy for aged women.
Like an offspring to the night,
like a friend to the Kali age,

A darkness spread forth, as if denying the existence of perceptible substances like the tenets of the Buddhists;

and as if bearing fruit within a forest of tamāla trees dense with thick, spreading foliage.
It seemed to quiver within the thick tresses of exceedingly beautiful women;
it appeared to be ground down by the rays of sapphire gems;
and it was excessively dense in the forested ravines of the dark shadows.
In those [forests] where swarms of bees were utterly destroyed by the most formidable, singular, and vast trees— trees distinguished by their haughty pride and exceedingly clear,
intense, and manifest skill; which were thick and terrible, and radiant with the coils of most voracious venomous serpents.

Then, as the darkness bowed down like the onset of the moon, its mass shattered by the threatening luster of the tusks of elephants intoxicated with rut— and appearing like cupped hands formed by closing blue lotuses—

They were exceedingly vast, like the masses of spray released by the circles of the terrifying world-elephants bent under the burden of the earth difficult to sustain; they were widespread like clusters of foam vomited by the horses of the sun, exhausted from wandering through the distant vault of heaven;

To the Creator, who was counting the universe with the fingernails of his moon-like hands upon the skin of the sky— dark as ink from the shadows— the stars appeared like zeros spread out because of the utter emptiness of the world;

and like pellets from the ballista of the Flower-Armed One.
Like clusters of foam from the ocean of the sky,
like five-fingered marks of satisfaction fashioned by Rati upon the courtyard of the heavens,
and like heaps of pearls from the necklace of the Fortune of the Firmament;
From the moon’s funeral pyre, the stars shone like fragments of the bones of Kāma scattered by the force of the wind;

they resembled parched grain seeds bursting while being roasted in the great cauldron of the vast expanse of the sky, which was darkened by the smoke of rising gloom and stained crimson by the twilight.
And with them, the sky appeared as if it were afflicted with leprosy.

it was a thief of the splendor of the circular mouth of Kandarpa’s golden quiver.

The Lord of Night, his orb reddened by the dawn, attained his rising; he bore the hue of the javā-flower blossoming upon the crest of the eastern mountain, appearing like the moonlight-embellished night’s vessel filled with pure saffron paste, or like the saffron-scarlet jar-like breast of the eastern quarter.

Like a white parasol for the god of love,
like a circle of ivory tusks for the great elephant of the sky,

Like a sandbank of the Yamunā at night,
like a crystal linga of the ascetic sky,
like the egg of the black serpent;
It was like a conch-shell of the great ocean of the sky;
like a shrine of the fish-bannered god of love after he had been consumed by the enemy of passion;
and like the circle of a funeral pyre of the mind-born god, variegated with the charcoal of his dark spot.
Like a white lotus moving through the sky,
like a mass of foam upon the great ocean of the atmosphere, or like a globule of mercury [according to those who propound the doctrine of the elixir of time].
Variegated like a silver pitcher with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass,
as beautiful as the wheel of Kāmadeva’s chariot,
he was the crest-jewel of the Eastern Mountain.
Like a pigeon upon the great palace of the sky, like the frontal globe of Airāvata,
or like an old bull with broken horns;
The moon, the lord of planets, rose like a white silver vessel slipped from the hand of a celestial maiden, appearing as the white wheat and rice of the field of the sky;
and he was the white lotus for the bees that were the eyes.
The sandy banks of the beds were for the swans of their hearts,
and the crystal fans were for the fires of their separation.
In the meantime, there arose the manifold, double-meaning, and fluctuating utterances of female messengers sent by groups of *abhisārikā* women to their beloveds.
For it is thus:
"You do not truly perceive yourself as having been stripped of womanhood;
you are as hard as a stone."
And you are not even one among the attractors, magnets, or liquefiers; you are merely a "mover," O rogue!
Like a mere thrower who has failed to apply the purpose of his efforts, you have needlessly carried a sword for too long.

With a mind as if full of sorrow, you contemplate that which is difficult to attain; yet he who acts with the essence of courage stands having attained tranquility at the forefront of the enemy host. He is indeed a hero who, through combat, leads away the elephants of the adversary.
Even one who maintains a multitude of broad-sworded arms attains this great calamity through conflict;

yet, O ornament of the earth, you are certainly not devoid of royal splendor, nor are you separated from the army. Your heroism, O crest-jewel of patience, is confident, clear as a cloudless sky, and capable of protecting against the pride of serpents; it is vast in its own greatness, and while your heroism resides in your mind, your truthfulness resides in your speech.

By her boldness and her smile, Kamalā, whose abode is the lotus, was conquered; she, who is dedicated to you and possesses a pure heart as clear as a mirror, with her lotus-like hand surpassing a tender sprout, appears as if her fingers were adorned with bracelets as she gazes again and again through the lattice of the window with playful grace,
experiencing sorrows that bring about her destruction.
O Lord of Life, who here would not take refuge in you, the auspicious one, for the sake of life?
Let other [servants] be set aside; even before them, I myself choose servitude.
Therefore, let there be friendship—friendship indeed!
By your very nature, you do not manifest even a slight pride that could rival the pride of Kandarpa; rather, death stands ever-present in its entirety.

O purifier of the wicked-minded, O enricher of fame, the attendants of her whose face has become manifest through servitude—attained by those whose side-glances are equally intense and irresistible, and who are captivated by love—are the very faces of women as beautiful as lotuses; yet by you, the faces of those women as beautiful as lotuses have been soiled.

Having attained the governance of every universe, you who have attained self-restraint perform for many ages a concert that is both harmonious and subtle; yet, O slender-limbed one, through the power of the flower-arrowed god of love, your passion having been aroused,
you wander for a moment and faint, your eyes dull with bashfulness—
O sweet-lipped woman, who, joined by a lover whose lips are as sweet as desire, possesses a moon-like face adorned with a distinctive mark of streaks of pollen.
Clasping you to her heart with a hand that is soft as a mine of tenderness, and with breasts whose nipples are like drops of perspiration upon golden breast-plates that surpass all turbid gold—

Madayantī, her eyes red with passion, desiring you who are composed of love and who delight in passion, longs for you, the most supreme lover, with a captivating charm that is cruel to the god of desire.
With her captivating jar-like breasts, her captivating eyes that stole the luster of deer-eyes, and her captivating [form],
the world rejoiced as if it had immediately entered the ocean of milk, as if it had entered a crystal palace, and as if it were experiencing the bliss of dwelling in Śvetadvīpa.

And gradually, as the evening breeze blew—thin and delicate; making the quarters of the sky resonant with the sweet warbling of swarms of bees longing for the abundance of honey-drops from the interior of the night-lotus groves whose petals were slowly parting; censuring the departure [of travelers] by means of female cakora birds languid from the weight of drinking moonlight; and removing the droplets of perspiration from the beautiful Pulinda women exhausted by the burden of lovemaking.
When the wind was like the sighs of the night, Kandarpaketu, accompanied by Tamālikā and Makaranda, went to the city of Vāsavadattā’s father.

Immediately thereafter, he beheld [the city] adorned with banners that shone like a host of deities who had arrived for the sake of seeing Vāsavadattā, wearing bracelets formed from fragments of pearls, *makaranda* gems, and rubies set in a secluded spot within a part of the camp; banners that seemed to threaten the splendor of the city of the sky with sprays of flowers from the celestial trees tossed by the wind.

With streams flowing from the stone pavements, carrying the fragrance of water perfumed with camphor, sandalwood, saffron, and cardamom; with flocks of palace pigeons sleeping soundly, unaware of their presence, as they rested comfortably upon crystal slabs on the banks; with waters made turbid by clusters of blossoms falling from the trees on the slopes; and with the sacrificial altars drenched by sprays of water tossed up by the constant splashing of the hips of intoxicated young women bathing therein.
[The rivers] with female royal swans whose presence was inferred by their calls as they sat upon banks formed of sand strewn with camphor;
who displayed, through groves of blooming blue lotuses, a sudden suspicion of darkness caused by cakravāka birds;
and who possessed beautiful breasts like young women.
[The city was] as if with the arts of battle of Sugrīva, for its elephants were drenched in ichor;
like the shores of the ocean, for they were variegated by the pollen from the feet of beautiful women; and like the mental states of a new king, for the female elephants moved like small streams.

It was adorned with palaces illuminated by clusters of peacocks that bore the form of glass jars, appearing as if they were supporting a multitude of stars that had come to gaze upon the young women under the guise of pearl nets atop their pinnacles;
and it displayed the swelling of untimely clouds through the masses of smoke from black aloe-wood incense.
In some places, the blue-necked peacocks were being slowly and gently danced into motion, summoned by the deep resonance of the drum;
it was like the evening hour when the eyes of the world have fallen asleep,
or like the sacrificial ground of Janaka when Rāma was eager for his bride.
Like human love made manifest, like a treasure-trove of curiosity,
and like the very dwelling-place of erotic passion.
He beheld the palace of Vāsavadattā, which was like a family home for delusion, a rendezvous for beauty, and possessed the splendor of the delight of the gods.

O Kalikā creeper, release this noisy girdle that is the cause of strife for me, so that we may hear the sweet sound of the lute.

it is you alone who, through your talkativeness, cause shame here. Let this innocent Avantisenā fall upon the offering of flowers; enough with your deceptive jests!
Lavaṅgikā: "The very trembling reveals your inner intent.

though covered, it serves as a welcome offering."
In your longing, there is a great wave of yearning;
tell me, what can serve as a comparison for the beauty of your face, which is to be drunk in by the eyes—even the moon falls short?
There dwells within your heart, which abides in the vow of chastity, some unknown being.

O Keralī, your speech, experienced as having a hundredfold essence with a hundred streams, has been realized. This mass of your hair, bearing a garland of blossoming jasmine flowers, attains the likeness of a fragment of a dark rain-cloud with its hands raised.
O Kuntalikā, the sounds of songs are heard coming from the vicinity of the city gate.
Why do you imagine this for a moment merely from the closing of your eyes? Furthermore, why do you weary your fickle friends who are eager for sport?

O Muralā, have you forgotten that joy which was obtained by striking your breasts with your breasts during amorous play—a joy that dispels the fever of love—and are you now bewildered because you are separated from him?

With the darkness of delusion destroyed, your beloved remembered your skill, which is so dear to Rati; yet the wound from your nails caused no pain to her during that night born of love. Why was that region of the night—which delights the eyes of all people with its two eyes—not drunk in by your two eyes?
Dear friend Madanamālinī, O Mālinī, cease your desire to abandon contact with Bimba’s lips!
What distinction is there between them and the surface of a Mālavī woman’s cheek, which is reddened by the intoxication of wine, being alike in its unswerving redness due to its circular hue?
Kuraṅgikā, prepare some young grass shoots for the fawns.

Mātaṅgikā, honor the request for the young elephant;
Śaśilekhā, draw the crescent moon upon the tablet of your forehead;
Ketakikā, provide the ritual treatment for the ketaka bower.
Śakunikā, give food to the pet birds.

Madanalekhā, write a love-letter for the Malaya breeze;
