Hearing these conversations, Kandarpaketu, together with Makaranda, felt astonishment in his mind: "Oh, how extraordinary is the beauty of these mansions!
Oh, what skill there is in the composition of erotic grace!"
For instance, reflecting on such things as: "This pavilion is constructed of lovely teeth, tender as the luster of the Mālava women's lips crushed in play at that time;

and here is this pet parrot, confined within a mechanical cage fashioned from camphor sticks," and so forth, he entered with his foot stained with red lac as if by the *Vyākaraṇa*, and with his [garment] like the *Mahābhārata*...
She shone with a pair of shanks as beautiful as the Sundarakāṇḍa of the Rāmāyaṇa composed by the divine poet, and she possessed a radiant waist like that of the science of prosody (Chandovicitih).

Like the science of astrology, she had the asterisms Hasta and Śravaṇā as her hands; like the established order of logic, she possessed the nature of Uddyotakara; and like the Buddhist liturgy, she was adorned with ornaments.

she possessed beautiful feet like the established tradition of the twice-born;

Like Somaprabhā, the queen of Brahmadatta;
like Anupamā, the female elephant of the world-elephant;
like the shore adorned with *tamāla* leaves.
He beheld Vāsavadattā, languid with passion like a young she-mule;
then, as Kandarpaketu drank her in with eyes dilated by joy, a surge of fainting robbed him of consciousness,

Then, having regained consciousness through the efforts of Makaranda’s female companions, the two of them sat together upon a single seat.
Thereupon, Kalāvatī—dearer to Vāsavadattā than her own life and the repository of all her confidence—spoke to Kandarpaketu:
"Noble son, this is no occasion for confidential conversation."
Therefore, it is described as being exceedingly light:
if the sky were to become a leaf for you, the ocean were to become a pen, Brahmā were to become a scribe,

And you have abandoned the kingdom; what more need be said? You have placed yourself in a perilous situation.

This daughter of our master, when the night had turned to dawn, was [intended] by her father—who feared the fault of her youth passing away—to be given in marriage out of anxiety to Puṣpaketu, the son of Vijayaketu, the emperor of the Vidyādharas.
"She must be given [to him]. She too has reflected thus: 'If Tamālikā does not return today taking that person with her, then I shall certainly lie down in the fire.'"
Thus, by the power of her own merit, this illustrious one has arrived at this place.

Then Kandarpaketu, trembling with fear yet as if submerged in the surging waves of the vast ocean of the nectar of joy, took leave of Vāsavadattā and dispatched Makaranda to that very city to search for news.

Accompanied by her, he departed from the city on a horse named Manojava, which was like a serpent ever moving toward its prey. and a region made loathsome by swarms of buzzing crickets filling the ground, fallen amidst pools of blood from the ears and noses of terrified victims impaled upon the points of spears.

Having passed through the cemetery enclosure—which was terrifying with the clanging sounds of human skulls crackling as they were consumed by the fire of funeral pyres; which resembled the hand of Śiva, with its body encircled by serpents, ashes, and the embers of the sacrificial fire of the skull-bowl; and which appeared like a supreme being, having been served by many circles of practitioners—she went forth.
In what seemed like a mere moment, it reached many hundreds of yojanas;
it was like the time of universal dissolution with its massed suns risen,
and like the state of the serpent kings with their infinite roots.
It was like the Sudharmā hall, with its owls perched at will;
like the service of virtuous men, rich in the fruits of prosperity;
and like the battlefield of the Mahābhārata, where Arjuna trees grew far and wide.
It was like the abode of the Puloma clan, possessing Indrāṇikās worthy of the Thousand-eyed One; it was like the mental disposition of Śūrapāla, frequented by Gaṇikārikās;
it was like the prosperity of the virtuous, with blossoming Aśoka, Sarala, and Punnāga trees.
In one place, she was like the play of a child, supported by her nurse; in another, she was like the mental state of Rāghava, consisting entirely of Vaidehī;
and in yet another, she was like the moment of churning the Ocean of Milk, with nectar surging forth.
In some places it was like the power of Nārāyaṇa, unconquered and acting at will; in others, it was like the eloquence of Vālmīki, which reveals the lineage of the Ikṣvākus;
and it was like Laṅkā, adorned with many palāśa trees.
It was like the army of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons, surrounded by a multitude of Arjuna’s arrows;
like the form of Nārāyaṇa, possessing many forms; and like the army of Sugrīva, attended by Panasa, Candana, Nala, and Kumuda.
In some places she was like a widow, yet adorned with vermilion tilakas and coral ornaments;
in other places she was like the army of the Kurus, presided over by Ulūka, Droṇa, and Śakuni, and joined by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
though adorned with unfading noble birth, she was of a contrary lineage.
Though she offered freedom from fear, she was terrifying;
though she was always beneficial and wholesome, she was filled with thickets; though she was frequented by six-footed creatures, she was not crowded by two-footed beings.
He entered the Vindhya forest, which, though adorned by families of the twice-born, was itself of ignoble lineage.

In the blooming lotus-pond, which resembled a red garment, was provided with a manuscript of hundred-petaled lotuses upon a bed of unevenly sprouted lotus-stalks, and which seemed to recite its own excellent colors through the deep, low humming of bees intoxicated by drinking their full from the abundance of honey-drops;
while the petals were closing like thick jars, and the filaments— muddy with sweet nectar— resembled the seeds of darkness sown by Time, who acted like a mendicant-farmer among the bees.
While the lotus-pond offered, as it were, incense to the Lord Sun—who is garlanded with rays—under the guise of its tall white lotuses followed by swarms of bees whose girdles were made of pollen;
while the moon was like a mortar whose interior was wounded by the blows of pestles leaping from the two hands of the bride Night;
and while the clusters of stars were emerging like grains of rice scattered during threshing.
As the monkey of the day, its face copper-red with the twilight, climbs the tree of the sky,
the clusters of stars fall like blossoms from the trembling branches of the quarters, and the orb of the moon falls like a fruit; then,
as the cock of the day— whose beautiful face is adorned by a crest of shimmering, deep red— descends to wander upon the courtyard of the sky, variegated with the rice-grains of the stars.

While the eastern quarter seemed to laugh, as it were, saying, "This lord of the twice-born, having become famous through association with me, shall fall due to his union with Vāruṇī," [the sky was reddened] by streams of blood from the elephant of darkness slain by the blow of the sun's rays, as if by the mineral dyes washed away from the peaks of the Eastern Mountain by mountain torrents,
or as if by the reflections of rubies split open by the hooves of galloping horses.

It was a crimson orb, as if it were a stream of blood flowing from the heads of intoxicated elephants struck by the palms of lions; as if it were filled with the essence of passion for the power of accomplishing the affairs of the three worlds;
and as if it had extended its hand, red as saffron dye, to seize the groves of night-lotuses that are the stars.
Upon the offering of the hood of the serpent-king of the eastern mountain by the playful maiden of the East;
upon the golden sprout of the sapphire-blue sky;
upon the golden coin-casket of the eastern wall of the city of the heavens.
It was like a moist drop of saffron upon the broad forehead of the East,
a solitary blossom on the young creeper of twilight,
resembling a silken thread reddened with madder.

As the blessed sun ascended, he was woven with the crimson of twilight like a golden coin from the eastern mountain; he was like a magic pill for the Vidyādhara and Siddha of the day, and like the footprints of the world-elephant reddened by mineral pigments, he was the thief of the darkness of night.
Like a smear of madder upon the fly-whisks of the world-elephants;
like the gushing blood from the battle of the Mahābhārata on the fields of Kurukṣetra;
like a coating of the splendor of Indra’s bow upon the fragments of clouds.
Like saffron robes in the small hermitage huts of the Śākyas,
like the safflower dye upon the fluttering ends of victory banners.
Like the ripening of the fruit on *karkandhu* trees,
like the essence of a streak of saffron upon the courtyard of the palace of the sky,
and like the moving curtain of crimson belonging to Time;
As the sunlight, red as the breaking of young sprouts,
spread forth— for a moment, as if to remove the fever of grief from the hearts of the flocks of *cakravāka* birds, or as if to enter into fire—

As the mass of rays of the hot-rayed sun rose, as if from contact with the sunstone beloved of the Lord of Day, Kandarpaketu took refuge in them; he was overcome by having stayed awake all night, his body was devoid of food and thus unconscious,
and he was exhausted from wandering for many hundreds of yojanas.

Together with Vāsavadattā, who was likewise in such a state, he slept in the bower of creepers— charming with the humming of bees wandering about, drawn by the fragrance of blossoms swaying in the gentle breeze— his entire collection of senses rendered motionless by the sleep natural to that hour.
Then, like a merchant upon the spread-out sky, or like a great forest fire consuming all the wood, the orb of the sun appeared.

When midday had arrived, Kandarpaketu, looking upon the bower of creepers in the absence of his beloved, rose up and cast his gaze here and there— momentarily upon the branches and momentarily upon the treetops.
For a moment in blind wells,
for a moment on heaps of dry leaves,
and for a moment in the sky.
Wandering for a moment toward the cardinal directions and for a moment toward the intermediate points, his heart burning incessantly, he lamented:
"Alas, my beloved Vāsavadattā! Grant me a sight of you!"
Why do you vanish in jest?
You alone are the measure of those sufferings that I have experienced on your account.
Dear friend Makaranda, behold my ill-fated turn of fortune!
What pure deed have I not performed?
Destiny is fraught with bitter fruit.
Difficult to overcome is the course of untimely death; alas, how bitter is the casting of the planets' glances! Alas, how incongruous is the fruit of the blessings of one's elders!
"Alas! The fruit of evil dreams and ill omens has ripened.
In every way, there is nothing that is beyond the reach of destiny.
Have the sciences not been correctly mastered?"
Have you not properly propitiated your gurus? Have you not attended upon the sacred fires?
Have you not worshipped the deities?
"Have the deities of the earth been insulted? Have the fragrant flowers not been circumambulated?

Has 'O Fearless One, refuge-seeker' not been uttered?"—lamenting thus in many ways, he emerged from the southern forest, which was thick with young *nalas*, *naladas*, lotus-pools, *niculas*, *piculas*, and *viḍudas*.
Its vicinity was enclosed by thickets of *ciribilva* and *bilva* trees and by *kuṭaja* shrubs;
its beautiful groves were made lovely by the humming of longing *bhṛṅgarāja* bees;
and it was filled with swarms of bees rising from the trunks of young *varuṇa* trees, which were themselves shrouded by a dense mass of spreading cane creepers.
The ground beneath the trees was drenched by the flow of honey from swarms of bees broken loose by langurs;
it was thick with *tāla*, *hintāla*, betel-nut, *punnāga*, and *nāgakesara* trees;
and dense with thickets of *ghanasāra*, jasmine, *ketaka*, *kovidāra*, *mandāra*, citron, *jambīra*, and rose-apple shrubs.
With its groves of *nandīnalas* rendered green by flocks of *pratyūha* and *dātyūha* cranes;
with its abundant mango sprouts occupied by throngs of sweet-voiced cuckoos with unimpaired throats;
and with its fierce and formidable [trees] frequented by broods of restless domestic cocks.
With rows of *kurabaka* flowers bristling with horripilation like a mass of coral,
with the ten directions being anointed by the loveliness of the tender shoots of red *aśoka*,
and with a burgeoning weight of greyish hue from the day caused by the spreading pollen of blossoming *kesara* flowers;
It was filled with the sweet warbling of bees drawn to flower-clusters yellowed by pollen, which brought joy to the people;
it contained the trunks of mucukunda trees, darkened by rut-fluid, where fearless elephants rubbed their temples to relieve their itching;
and its hollows within the *kuṭaja* trees were occupied by hens that had recently laid eggs.
It was a place where the clever chatter of sparrows being led about by their mates performed constant endearments;
where the cakora birds, expert in wandering with their female companions, were ever intent on their duties;
and where young fawns lay happily upon stone slabs as tender as *śaileya* herbs.
With multitudes of mongooses dwelling with confidence in the hollows of the roots of *śephālikā* shrubs,
free from the fear of *raṅkuṇa* insects, and where the play of mongooses was undisturbed;

With the emergence of mango buds swallowed by flocks of black cuckoos; with herds of *camara* yaks chewing the cud like groves of mango trees; and with the drumbeats of the ear-flaps of elephant herds—sluggish in their joy from sleep induced by the sound of waterfalls on the mountain slopes near their nests, which are as enchanting to the ear as the notes of the cuckoo.

It was filled with herds of ruru deer delighting in the excellent songs of nearby kinnarīs; it was protected by young boars whose snouts were stained by the juice of green turmeric crushed by them; and it was teeming with mongooses making a humming sound amidst clusters of guñjā berries.

Having traveled a short distance along the shore of the great ocean, which was crowded with clusters of *pāṭala* insects torn open by the beaks of ten enraged young monkeys, and where herds of lions— resplendent with beautiful manes smeared by streaks of blood from intoxicated elephants split by fierce slaps from the tips of their claws as hard as the peak of a thunderbolt— [dwelt].
It was skilled in mimicking the battle-axe of Śiva with its mass of dancing, uplifted arms, due to the accumulation of its restless waves;

its beauty along the shores was enhanced by rows of foam that resembled the victory banners of Varuṇī, the flower-clusters from the sloughs of the serpent Śeṣa, or the continuous stream of atoms remaining after the moon had been consumed;
like another sky descended to the surface of the earth under the guise of the clear ocean, it seemed to entice the sky-dwellers with pearls in the form of rising sprays of water droplets.
Its interior was filled with many winged mountains that had come seeking protection;
it contained the excavated pit of Sagara’s sons,
from which the Pārijāta tree had been uprooted.
A source of noble jewel-gems,
teeming with schools of dolphins and sea-monsters,
and longing to swallow large fish.
It was a sea where the wheels of wandering ships moved about;
where clusters of *lavalī*, clove, and *mātuluṅga* trees were tossed about by the circling rings of schools of whales that had set down;
and where young moss on the sandy banks was crushed by pairs of water-nymphs, who were agitated by the tall *tālī* palms trembling from the wind of the waves.
Its rocky slopes were inscribed with lines by the harsh claws of crabs, whose mouths were torn open by the tips of coral sprouts;
its waters were thick with flocks of birds of the lineage of the Lord of Birds;
and it still seemed not to have released the momentum of the Mandara-churning, as evidenced by the whirling of its eddies.
It was as if full of reproach through its foam,
as if filled with the fragrance of wine through the scent of the *bakula* trees on the shore,
and as if full of wrath through its thunders.
As if sighing with grief,
as if knitting its brows with its waves,
and as if tethering itself to a mooring pillar by means of Rāma’s bridge.
Like the belly of Kumbhīnasī, it was the source of salt;
like grammar, it abounded in the extensive application of feminine suffixes;
like a royal court, it displayed great vessels of state.
It was like a stable for elephants, with many serpents emerging from the water with hissing sounds;
it was like the host of Viśvāmitra’s sons, adorned by beautiful fish as lovely as lotuses;
it was like a virtuous man, taking refuge in his lineage, and like a holy man, made charming by the steadfastness of the Imperishable One (Viṣṇu).
It was like a virtuous king accompanied by his noble ministers,
like one whose anger has been appeased with a bath in the Karatoyā river,
and like a lover in separation sprinkled with sandalwood water.
Like a dandy immersed in the Narmadā river;
though having extracted the Kālakūṭa poison, still manifesting heaps of ashes;
and though extremely aged, yet with his neck embraced by a beautiful woman.
He beheld the ocean, the birthplace of the gods and the abode of the asuras.
He thought to himself: "Aha! Even by Fate, who has done me such injury, a favor has been rendered, in that this ocean has been brought within the range of my vision.
Therefore, casting off my body here, I shall extinguish the fire of separation from my beloved."
Even though the relinquishing of one's life is not prescribed for one who is not ill, it must nevertheless be performed;
for indeed, not everyone performs every action, whether it be something that ought to be done or something that ought not to be done.
In this essence-less cycle of existence, what indeed has not been done by whom?
For instance:
the King of the Twice-born (Bṛhaspati) abducted the wife of his guru;
Purūravas perished through his greed for the wealth of a brahmin.
Nahuṣa became a great serpent through his longing for another's wife;
Yayāti fell after having taken a hand in marriage;
Sudyumna became as if composed entirely of womanhood.
Soma was notorious for his mercilessness in killing living beings;
Purukutsa was as if contemptible;
and Kuvalayāśva even carried off the daughter of an ass.
Nṛga became a lizard;
Kali overcame Nala;
Saṃvaraṇa fell into a state of dejection regarding the daughter of Mitrā.
Daśaratha met his death through the madness of excessive attachment to Rāma;
Kārtavīrya went to his destruction by oppressing cows and Brahmins;
and Manu perished through his addiction to gold.
Śāntanu lamented in the forest due to excessive grief;
Yudhiṣṭhira uttered the truth at the head of the battle;
indeed, there is almost no one who is entirely without blemish.

Thinking, "I shall not be stained by blame upon the abandonment of this body," he [beheld] a place where the surface was muddied by the thick, broad scales torn by the tips of the sharp talons of ospreys; where the water was filled with the cries of flocks of otters crowded together among the scales of dense śakula fish; and whose banks were lined with a succession of the shells of crabs, the leavings of packs of jackals.
It was made turbid by the swallowing of schools of darting minnows tossed about by the exceedingly rapid current of the water;
its surroundings were whitened by flocks of very silent cranes;
and it was cooled, refreshed, and made fragrant by the spray of water droplets stirred up by the sporting of swarms of extremely restless water-fowls.

Its rugged slopes were scarred by the tips of the horns of very young forest buffaloes falling there day after day; it resounded with the sweet cries of flocks of birds with white faces and feet that wandered there incessantly;
and its surface of the earth was like a mass of water shimmering in the rays of the sun, as if the clouds had been crushed beneath the bed of Manu.
It was a place where swarms of bees, drawn by the sweet humming of hundreds of noble elephants whose temples were dappled with the exceedingly thick ichor of rut, descended;
its shores were covered with clusters of gems fallen from the breaking of water tossed by the exceedingly swift wind;
it resembled, as it were, the slough cast off by the serpent that is the ocean.
Like a mirror for the earth,
he reached the sandy shore of Varuṇa, which was like a floor of crystal;
then, having performed his ablutions and other rites, he began to descend into the water to abandon his body.
48) Then, among the crocodiles that were benevolent, among the fish that were free from envy,
and among the small creatures that were not mean-spirited,
The tortoises were affectionate,
the crocodiles were free from cruelty,
and the sea-monsters were granters of fearlessness.
While we were among the crocodiles,
Sarasvatī emerged from the sky,
saying: "Noble Kandarpaketu, you shall again be united with your beloved before long."
"Therefore, desist from this resolve for death.
Having heard this, he ceased his efforts toward dying.
Then, with the hope of reunion with his beloved, he went to the ground at the edge of the marsh, desiring to take food as a means for sustaining his life.
There, wandering here and there and subsisting on fruits, roots, and the like in the forest, he passed his time.
One day, after several months had elapsed, [the forest] resounded with the roar of full-flowing rivers like a singer with a sweet, high-pitched voice;
it was like the hour of twilight when the peacocks are dancing.
Like Kumāra with his peacock, he bore the thunderbolt;
like a great ascetic, he had stilled the spreading of passion (rajas);
like an ascetic, he held the water-pot of the clouds.
The rainy season arrived, displaying the illusion of many suns as if at the time of universal dissolution;
it was like a region of a forest free from danger where deer were intensely eager,
and its hand was held by Balarāma like the sprout-like hand of Revatī.

50) In the sky, which was like a pleasure-lake with forests of split clouds and blue lotuses, it was like a jeweled ship for the God of Love; like a swinging rope for the dancing of the elephant-daughters that are unchaste women;
and like a garland for the archway of the palace of the heavens.
By Anidāgha, while traveling abroad, [the sky] was marked with a row of nail-scratches as if for remembrance upon the breast of the day’s cloud;
it was like a string of gems on the jeweled girdle of the Fortune of the Sky,
and like a cluster of blossoms from the Mandāra tree of the firmament.
Like a jeweled probe for polishing the nails of the Night,

like a jewel-encrusted oyster shell of the God of the Flowered Banner, the rainbow-staff shone forth. (51) A mass of clouds appeared as if it were vomiting up the garland of conchs from the ocean, which had been swallowed with excessive speed, under the guise of cranes.
In the black fields and small plots turned yellowish-green, the rainy season played with the frogs leaping up like speckled jewels, as if in rivalry with the lightning.
Upon the cloud, which was like a touchstone for the mass of soot from the lamp of the sun, the lightning shone like a streak of gold polished by a master goldsmith at that time.
Like a saw-blade of the flower-armed god, it appeared as a saw-teethed shield to tear open the hearts of those separated from their lovers.
In the clouds, which were torn asunder by the falling leaves of flickering lightning-stalks, the water-dust, shaken by the force [of the wind], appeared like heaps of powder;

and the hailstones shone like handfuls of parched grain for Makaradhvaja, who desires to conquer the world, scattered from the broken necklaces of the maiden-like quarters when crushed by the collision of dense clouds whirled by the force of the harsh wind.

52) Immediately thereafter, [he went] to a place where the *khañjarīṭa* birds were not limping, where the *krauñca* cranes moved without bending, where the branches resounded with the chatter of *bharadvāja* birds in full abundance, and where the fields of rice were filled with parrots and *kalama* paddy moving about like vessels.
In which royal swans had entered as guests,
where the ground was radiant with the luster of the body of the enemy of Kaṃsa, and where the shimmering clouds were equal to swan’s down;

In that place where the great lover, the moon, was made dense with joy; where the grasses and creepers were sweet with honey; and where the lakes had their essence consisting of the cries of joyful cranes;

Delighting in the sweet sounds of the bees swarming over the clusters of leaves belonging to the *māṣaputrī* plants moving along the banks and ponds that had been uprooted by the young elephants— sons and grandsons of those lusting after the *kaśeruka* and *kandala* roots;
while the *kadamba* trees were being tormented and the enemies of the conch (the peacocks) were distressed, yet the lotus stalks were spreading their blossoms.
When the cātaka birds are trembling with fear, when the clouds are sparse, and when the stars shine with increasing brilliance;
In the lovely moonlight of the western quarter,
amidst waters of sweet flavor,
where minnows dart and the tips of fishing poles quiver;
In a circle of owls and frogs,
with their bodies drawn into their shells,
appearing pale like fragments of gold.
In Krośadutkrośa,
Surabhigandhi, Saugandhika, Gandhahārin, Hariṇāśva, Kumudāmodin, Kaumudīkṛtamuda,
and Nibarhabarhin;
Where the lapwings warble,
the peacocks are held in check,
and the herds of deer are made happy by the songs of joyful female rice-wardens;
When the *kiṃśuka* trees were made to speak by the birds,
when the buds of the *mālatī* and *latā* vines were withered, and when the *bandhūka* flowers became companions [to the setting sun].
When the muñja grass had begun to sprout,
when the bows for the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice were strung,
and when the quarters of the sky were turned tawny by the pollen of blooming saffron flowers;
At the onset of the autumn season, when the white lotuses were in full bloom, Kandarpaketu, while wandering about, [beheld] a stone statuette out of curiosity,
delusion,
and grief.
With impetuosity, he touched her with his hand, thinking, "She is imitating my beloved.
Immediately upon being touched, she cast off her stone form and once again assumed the true appearance of Vāsavadattā.
Beholding her, Kandarpaketu, as if immersed in an ocean of nectar, embraced her for a long time and asked:
"My dear, tell me, what is this matter?
She, however, sighing long and hot, began to speak.

“O noble son, for the sake of me, an unfortunate and ill-fated woman, you, O illustrious one, having abandoned your kingdom, have experienced a suffering beyond the reach of speech or mind, like a solitary man.

For many days, being utterly devoid of food, you have become exceedingly emaciated; yet, thinking that if at the end of your sleep you should happen to find some fruit, root, or the like, you might maintain your body, you have been searching for fruit, looking toward the trees of the grove, and have come within the range of my sight.”
55) And in due course, there was the carrying away of the bodies performed while hidden by thickets, the construction of temples for Īśvara,
and the lowering of neck-ornaments.
where the sharp clatter of hooves was beginning to be heard, where the quarters for courtesans were being laid out, and where the neighing of horses could be heard;

I beheld the military encampment, where the drums and kettledrums were being sounded and then silenced, where reservoirs of sweet water were being sought out, and where the banners of the market-stalls were being pointed out.
Beholding him, I thought:

"Is this my father’s array for the sake of searching for me, or is it my noble husband’s military force? While I was thus reflecting, the commander-in-chief, having been informed of the news by his attendants, rushed toward me.
Immediately thereafter, the commander of the Kirāta army, accompanied by a similar force, arrived under the pretext of hunting; he too was terrified.
Then I thought:
"If I tell my noble son [of this], he will certainly be killed by these men while all alone."

"If I do not speak now, then I alone must be slain by these men"— at the very moment of this thought, a battle broke out between the two armies like that of two vultures competing for a single piece of meat.
Then, as the rays of the sun were obscured by the rainy day of the onset of a torrent of counter-arrows,
and as the illusory Vidyādharas were embraced by heroic warriors who, skilled in chariot warfare, held swords aloft on the trunks of elephants tossed far into the air;
In that place, where circles of celestial *cāraṇa* spirits moved about beholding the battle;

where groups of headless trunks (*kabandha*) overtaken by *vetāla* demons performed graceful movements; and where there was the spectacle of the mortars used as ear-ornaments for *piśācī* spirits, fashioned from the feet of elephants severed by the swords of fierce warriors.
In that battlefield, where the lotus-beds were in full bloom, where the drums of victory resounded, and where the cowards were fleeing in terror;

Regarding morsels of flesh bitten by the teeth of calves as if they were bits of meat craved by jackals, and regarding bodies bitten by serpents as if they were mere blades of grass, they maintained a sense of detachment; they drew the strings of their bows with the same indifference as they did the lives of their enemies. Like generous donors who cannot endure the distress of supplicants, the horses—like enraged great deer—shed their patience and shone forth.

With ears eager to hear the slander of others, with eyes that gazed upon the misfortunes of the virtuous, and with a head bowing down in the wrong place, the headless trunk (kabandha) danced for a long time out of sheer joy, thinking, "I have been abandoned!"
58) Then, as if in jest, he closed his eyes; as if reddened by hearing the slanders of others, he blocked the function of his ears; as if intoxicated, he was tossed about by the force of the wind;
and he acted like a bringer of gray hair to the celestial nymphs.
Like a blinding darkness for the warriors,
like the gloom of nightfall upon the battlefield,
it was as if fallen and its lineage cast off.

The battle-field expanded like the Mīmāṃsaka philosophy which has cast aside the Digambara doctrine, or like a virtuous man who, having taken refuge at the feet of Viṣṇu, is free from the dust of passion.
In that mass of combat, a certain warrior, fearing a broken thigh like Suyodhana, plunged into the water.
One lay for a long time gasping like Bhīṣma upon a bed of arrows;
another, with all his limbs paralyzed like Karṇa, discharged a spear.

Then that entire army, its banner-cloths shattered, its flags falling, its bows, chowries, and crests cast down, and its small swords slipping from grasp, met their destruction at one another's hands.

59) Immediately thereafter, the sage who owned that hermitage returned having gathered flowers and other offerings; having learned the entire sequence of events, he cursed her, saying, "Since this hermitage of mine has been destroyed, become a stone! However, immediately after, out of compassion, thinking, "This poor woman is undergoing great suffering," he brought an end to the curse, making it last only until she was touched by the noble son. 60) Then Kandarpaketu, having returned with Makaranda and Vāsavadattā to his own city, spent his time experiencing various pleasures of love as desired by his heart.
Thus ends the tale named *Vāsavadattā*, composed by the great poet Subandhu.
